## 

![](images/clipboard-2133479479.png){width="100"}

**Goal** Does owning a smartphone influences sleep, depression, obesity?

## What we know - Linear Regression

$$
y = \beta_0 + \beta_1x_1 + \beta_2x_2+\dots+\epsilon, \qquad \epsilon\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^2)
$$

- The [response]{.underline} is continuous (hours of sleep)

- The [predictors]{.underline} can be continuous of categorical (age, phone ownership, etc)

- The effects of the predictos act on the mean of the response.

. . .

**Example**

> If age uncreases by one year, keeping all other predictors constant, the mean slept hours decreases by $\beta$

## Group Discussion {.smaller}

::::: columns
::: {.column width="40%"}
Our response is the answer to:

> Does the child sleep less than 9 hours per night? Yes/No

Our predictor:

> hours of smartphone use per day.
:::

::: {.column width="60%"}
```{r}
library(tidyverse)
library(ggeasy)

set.seed(123)

n <- 300

hours <- runif(n, 0, 10)

eta <- -4 + 0.8 * hours
p <- plogis(eta)

df <- data.frame(
  hours,
  y = rbinom(n, 1, p))

df %>% ggplot() + geom_point(aes(hours, y)) + xlab(" hours of smartphone use per day") +
  ylab("Sleep less than 9hours")
```
:::
:::::

**Discuss**

- What should a good model predict?

- Can we use linear regression?

- Do you see any possible problem/challenge with linear regression?

## The model {.smaller}

- We want the model to predict probabilities!

- We want a linear predictor of the form $\beta_0 + \beta_1 x_1 + \beta_2 x_2 + \dots$

. . .

Let's try to fit a linear regression: $y =\beta_0 + \beta_1x +\epsilon$

```{r}
lm_fit  <- lm(y ~ hours, data = df)

glm_fit <- glm(
  y ~ hours,
  family = binomial,
  data = df
)

grid <- data.frame(
  hours = seq(0, 10, length.out = 200)
)

grid$lm_pred  <- predict(lm_fit, grid)


ggplot(df, aes(hours, y)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_line(
    data = grid,
    aes(hours, lm_pred,
        colour = "Linear regression"),
    linewidth = 1.2
  )  +  labs(
    y = "Probability of depression",
    colour = ""
  ) + xlab(" hours of smartphone use per day") + easy_remove_legend()
```

## Logistic Regression

We want to find a function of the probability to link to the linear predictor such that the predicted values always make sense!

. . .

```{r}

lm_fit  <- lm(y ~ hours, data = df)

glm_fit <- glm(
  y ~ hours,
  family = binomial,
  data = df
)

grid <- data.frame(
  hours = seq(0, 10, length.out = 200)
)

grid$lm_pred  <- predict(lm_fit, grid)
grid$glm_pred <- predict(glm_fit, grid,
                         type = "response")

ggplot(df, aes(hours, y)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_line(
    data = grid,
    aes(hours, lm_pred,
        colour = "Linear regression"),
    linewidth = 1.2
  ) +
  geom_line(
    data = grid,
    aes(hours, glm_pred,
        colour = "Logistic regression"),
    linewidth = 1.2
  ) +
  scale_colour_manual(
    values = c(
      "Linear regression" = "red",
      "Logistic regression" = "blue"
    )
  ) +
  labs(
    y = "Probability of depression",
    colour = ""
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

```

## From probabilities to odds

> Odds are just another way to express probabilities!

Assume we have 100 childred, 20 sleep less than hours are 80 more.

- What is the probability that a randomly selected child sleeps less than 9 hours?

## From probabilities to odds{.smaller}

> Odds are just another way to express probabilities!

. . .

Assume we have 100 childred, 20 sleep less than hours are 80 more.

- What is the probability that a randomly selected child sleeps less than 9 hours? $\frac{20}{100} = 0.2$

. . .

- For every child who sleeps less than 9 hours, how many sleep at least 9 hours? $\frac{20}{80} = 0.25$

. . .

$$
\text{Odds} = \frac{\text{number of events}}{\text{number of non-events}} = \frac{p}{1-p}
$$

## Compute the odds

| Probability | Odds |
|-------------|------|
| 0.5         |      |
| 0.1         |      |
| 0.9         |      |


- What do odds equal to 4 mean?

## Compute the odds

| Probability | Odds |
|-------------|------|
| 0.5         |   1   |
| 0.1         |   0.111   |
| 0.9         |    9   |

- Four children sleeping less than 9 hours for every one child who sleeps at least 9 hours.

## Odds and probability

```{r}
prob <- seq(0.01, 0.99, length.out = 200)

tibble(
  prob = prob,
  odds = prob/(1-prob)
) |>
ggplot(aes(prob, odds)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.2) +
  labs(
    x = "Probability",
    y = "Odds"
  )
```


## Log Odds and probability

```{r}
prob <- seq(0.001, 0.999, length.out = 200)

tibble(
  prob = prob,
  odds = log(prob/(1-prob))
) |>
ggplot(aes(prob, odds)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.2) +
  labs(
    x = "Probability",
    y = "log Odds"
  )
```



## Linear and logistic regression{.smaller}

::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
Linear Regression
$$
y = \beta_0 + \beta_1x + \epsilon
$$

- Response is continuous

- Covariates act linearly on the mean

:::

::: {.column width="50%"}

Logistic Regression
$$
\log\left(\frac{p}{1-p}\right) = \beta_0 + \beta_1x 
$$

- Response is binary (0/1)
- Covariates act linearly on the odds
:::
:::::

. . .

What they have in common:

- Clear model assumptions
- Simple and rigid relation between covariates and response
- Few parameters ( #covariates $\ll$ #observations)
- The parameters are interpretable

. . .

What comes in the next weeks (ML models):

- (Much) More flexible models
- Many more parameters
